title: India Clears 26 New Border Roads in Arunachal, The Hindu Reports
excerpt: The Cabinet Committee on Security reportedly cleared ICBR-III along the LAC earlier this year, with 33 ITBP bridges sanctioned since September, even as Eastern Sector talks and face-offs continue side by side.
body:
• The Cabinet Committee on Security cleared the third phase of the India-China Border Roads project, ICBR-III, covering 26 roads along the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh, a senior official told The Hindu; the government has not officially announced it.
  • Since September, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police has sanctioned 15 pedestrian suspension bridges and 18 log bridges in Upper Subansiri and Kurung Kumey districts, according to The Hindu's reporting.
  • The build-out runs alongside diplomacy: India and China held their first Corps Commander-level talks in the Eastern Sector at Wacha-Damai on September 6-7, while the ITBP chief said on October 22 that face-offs were continuing at several places in Arunachal.
  • Roads and bridges decide how long patrols can stay forward in Arunachal, where long-range patrols run only from June to October because snow closes the high ground for the rest of the year.

India has cleared a fresh round of infrastructure along its disputed border with China in Arunachal Pradesh without announcing it publicly, according to The Hindu. Citing a senior official, the newspaper reported that the Cabinet Committee on Security cleared the third phase of the India-China Border Roads project, ICBR-III, earlier this year — in February 2026, according to summaries of the report — covering 26 roads along the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh. The Union government has not officially announced the project or publicly disclosed its details, so the clearance should be understood as reported, not proclaimed.

What has been sanctioned

The roads are only part of the package described in the reporting. Since September, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, which guards the 3,488 km LAC under the Home Ministry, has sanctioned 15 pedestrian suspension bridges and 18 log bridges in Upper Subansiri and Kurung Kumey, two Arunachal districts bordering China. Those smaller links matter in terrain where a patrol's reach is set by whether it can cross a gorge without a multi-day detour. The new phase follows a long build-up: ICBR Phase I began in 2005 with 27 priority roads totalling 608 km to be built by the Home Ministry, and Phase II, approved on September 21, 2020 with an outlay of Rs 12,434.90 crore, covered 32 roads totalling 683 km and followed the June 2020 Galwan clashes in eastern Ladakh. In December 2020 the Home Ministry also approved 18 pedestrian tracks totalling 598.27 km in Arunachal border areas.

Talking and building at the same time

The infrastructure push runs parallel to renewed military diplomacy. India and China have held three rounds of engagement since July, including the first Corps Commander-level meeting in the Eastern Sector, at Wacha on September 6 and Damai on September 7, led for India by Lt Gen Girish Kalia of 3 Corps. Such talks had earlier been held mostly at Chushul-Moldo in Ladakh. Yet on October 22, ITBP Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said face-offs were continuing at several places in Arunachal, and the reporting says face-offs with Chinese troops in Arunachal have continued since late July. The pattern is two-track: dialogue to manage incidents, and infrastructure to change the ground conditions under which the next incident is handled.

Why roads decide presence

A frontier is held by people being present, and presence depends on how fast supplies can reach the edge. In Arunachal, long-range patrols operate only from June to October; snow closes the high ground for the rest of the year. A road or bridge cuts a multi-day trek to hours, so patrols last longer, posts can be resupplied, and reinforcements can arrive before a standoff hardens. That is the practical meaning of 26 roads and 33 small bridges. The comparison on the other side is China's Xiaokang border villages — including a roughly 100-home settlement built in the disputed Tsari Chu valley in 2020 — which combine civilian housing with military utility. India's parallel civilian-presence programme is the Vibrant Villages Programme, with Rs 4,800 crore for 2,967 villages, alongside all-weather links such as the Sela Tunnel to Tawang, which opened in March 2024.

The cost of saying nothing

Silence has a security logic near a disputed line: announcing exact alignments tells the other side where to look and can invite protest during delicate talks. It also has costs. Without an announcement, Parliament and the public cannot track budgets or delivery on a programme whose earlier phases slipped for years — Phase II was approved 15 years after Phase I began — and border residents learn about projects late. For readers, the distinction is simple: a senior official has described a clearance to The Hindu; no official announcement, outlay or timeline for ICBR-III has been published. What to watch is whether the government confirms the phase and whether the Wacha-Damai talks produce a second round while building continues.
